lessons.title: Legal Housekeeping Before You Raise: Company Structure, DPIIT Recognition and Founder Agreements

children.text: Deals rarely die because a founder gave a bad answer in a meeting. They die in week six, when a lawyer opens the folder and finds the app was built by a freelancer who never signed anything, a co-founder who left last year still holds 25%, and three employees have ESOP promises that exist only in WhatsApp. None of that is hard to fix in advance, and all of it is expensive to fix under deal pressure. This lesson is the boring work that keeps a term sheet alive.

body.text: Investors do not fund ideas, they buy shares in a legal entity. If that entity does not cleanly own its people, its code and its own share register, there is nothing safe to buy, however good the business is.

children.text: Start With the Right Entity

Equity investors buy shares. Only a company can issue them, which is why almost every funded Indian startup is a private limited company under the Companies Act, 2013. A proprietorship or partnership has no shares to sell. An LLP has partnership interests, which VC funds and angel funds generally will not take, and converting an LLP into a company mid-raise adds months you will not have.

body.text: Incorporating early is cheap. Incorporating in a hurry is not. If you plan to raise within a year, register the private limited company now, open the bank account, appoint the auditor and start filing properly. A company with two clean years of records is worth more in diligence than a company with two clever years of stories.

children.text: Founder Agreements and Vesting

markDefs.definition: An arrangement where founder shares are earned over time. If the founder leaves early, the company can buy back the unearned shares at a nominal price.
An initial period, usually one year, during which nothing vests. Leave before the cliff and you keep nothing.

children.text: The single most damaging thing early founders do is split equity on day one with no conditions attached. The fix is
founder vesting
, usually over four years with a one-year
cliff

and monthly vesting after that. Investors will insist on it anyway at the first priced round, often restarting the clock. Doing it yourself, early, means you set the terms instead of accepting theirs.
Three co-founders split a company 40:30:30 with no vesting. Fourteen months in, the 30% co-founder takes a job in Dubai and stops working. He keeps 30% forever, for 14 months of work.

The damage compounds. The two who stay now build the company for someone who left. Any investor looking at the cap table sees a large passive holder, which is a red flag they will want fixed before investing. Fixing it later means negotiating a buyback with someone who has every incentive to refuse.

With standard four-year vesting and a one-year cliff, he would have earned 14 ÷ 48 of his 30%, which is 8.75%. The remaining 21.25% returns to the company for the people still doing the work. Same story, completely different outcome, decided by a document signed when everyone was still friends.

body.title: How much has actually been earned?
body.prompt: A co-founder holds 30,00,000 shares on a four-year vesting schedule with a one-year cliff and monthly vesting thereafter. She resigns exactly 18 months after the start date. How many shares have vested?
body.explanation: She crossed the one-year cliff, so vesting applies on a monthly basis: 30,00,000 × 18 ÷ 48 = 11,25,000 shares. The other 18,75,000 shares are unvested and can be bought back by the company at a nominal price under the founder agreement. Had she left at month 11, before the cliff, she would have kept nothing.

children.text: A founders' agreement should settle six things while the relationship is good: the equity split and vesting, who decides what, what full-time commitment means, how a founder can exit, what happens to their shares when they do, and the fact that everything each founder creates belongs to the company.
Does the Company Own What It Sells?

In India, work created by an employee in the course of employment generally belongs to the employer, but a freelancer or agency usually keeps the rights unless the contract assigns them. Most early startups are built partly by freelancers. That means the code, designs and content an investor thinks they are buying may legally sit with a contractor in another city who was paid ₹40,000 two years ago.

stats.label: Employment contracts
stats.context: Signed by every employee, including the founders themselves

stats.label: Contractor agreements
stats.context: Get these signed even retrospectively, before diligence starts

stats.label: Trademark
stats.context: File early. A ₹10,000 filing avoids rebranding after a legal notice

stats.label: Domains and accounts
stats.context: Not in a co-founder's personal email or a former intern's account

body.text: Check who owns your GitHub repositories, cloud accounts, domain names, app store listings, payment gateway account and analytics logins. A startup where a departed employee still controls the production server is not fundable, and the discovery usually happens at the worst possible moment.

children.text: Keep the Cap Table and Filings Clean

Diligence will compare what you say you own with what the Registrar of Companies says you own. Those two must match exactly. That means share certificates issued, the register of members updated, allotment returns filed after every issue of shares, board and shareholder resolutions signed and dated, the statutory auditor appointed, annual financial statements and returns filed on time, and GST and TDS current. Most private companies other than small companies are now also required to hold and issue their shares in dematerialised form, so check whether that applies to you.

body.label: MCA: View Company or LLP Master Data
body.description: Look up your own company exactly as an investor's lawyer will: incorporation details, authorised and paid-up capital, directors and whether your filings are up to date.

body.text: Never promise equity or ESOPs in an email, a WhatsApp message or a conversation. Every promise creates an expectation that will surface in diligence, and a cap table that does not reconcile with what employees believe they own has ended rounds. Grant ESOPs only through a board-approved and shareholder-approved scheme, with a signed grant letter for each employee.

children.text: DPIIT Recognition Under Startup India

Recognition by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade is free, applied for online, and is the gate to most central startup benefits. It does not give you money by itself, but without it several doors stay shut.

body.caption: DPIIT recognition: who qualifies and what it unlocks

cells: Incorporated as a private limited company, registered partnership firm or LLP
Eligibility to apply for the Startup India Seed Fund Scheme through approved incubators
Up to 10 years old from the date of incorporation
Access to the Credit Guarantee Scheme for Startups, so lenders can lend without conventional collateral
Turnover has not exceeded ₹100 crore in any financial year since incorporation
Eligibility to apply for the startup profit-linked tax holiday, subject to a separate Inter-Ministerial Board certificate
Working on innovation or improvement of products, processes or services, or a scalable model with high potential for employment or wealth creation
Faster patent and trademark processing with fee rebates, through facilitators
Not formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business
Self-certification under several labour and environment laws, and relaxed norms in public procurement

body.label: Recognition is not the tax holiday
body.context: DPIIT recognition is the first step. The startup profit-linked deduction, long known by its Income-tax Act, 1961 section number 80-IAC, needs a further approval from the Inter-Ministerial Board, and only a small share of recognised startups receive it. Check the section reference and eligibility window under the current Income-tax Act with your tax adviser before relying on it.

body.title: Which company cannot get DPIIT recognition?
body.question: Four Indian companies apply for DPIIT startup recognition. Which one is most clearly ineligible?
options: A three-year-old private limited company with ₹12 crore of turnover building warehouse robotics
An eight-year-old LLP with ₹40 crore of turnover running a subscription learning platform
A two-year-old private limited company formed by transferring an existing family trading business into it, doing the same work as before
A one-year-old private limited company with no revenue developing a battery diagnostics device
body.explanation: An entity formed by splitting up or reconstructing an existing business is specifically excluded, and doing the same trading work under a new name is not innovation. The others are within the age and turnover conditions, and having no revenue yet is not a disqualification.

body.title: Six weeks into diligence
body.scenario: Zenta Labs has a signed term sheet for a ₹22 crore Series A. In diligence the investor's lawyers find four things. One: the mobile app was built in year one by a Pune agency whose contract has no IP assignment clause. Two: a co-founder who left 20 months ago holds 18% with no vesting agreement. Three: eleven employees hold offer letters promising ESOPs worth "1% of the company", but no ESOP scheme has ever been approved. Four: the brand name is unregistered, and a Delhi company has a pending trademark application for a near-identical name.
body.prompt: Which of these is most likely to kill the deal, and in what order should the founders tackle them?
body.modelAnswer:
Ranked by threat to the deal:
1. The IP gap is the most dangerous, because it goes to whether the company owns the asset being bought. Fix first: go back to the Pune agency and get a written assignment of all deliverables, backdated in effect through a confirmatory deed. Expect to pay something. Their leverage rises the moment they learn a round is closing, so approach it as routine housekeeping and move quickly.
2. The departed co-founder's 18% is next. Investors will not fund a company where a large passive holder contributes nothing. Options: negotiate a buyback, agree a reduced stake, or in the worst case accept the dilution and let the investor reprice the round. There is no clean fix under time pressure, which is exactly why vesting exists at incorporation.
3. The ESOP promises create a gap between the cap table and eleven people's expectations. Adopt a proper scheme with board and shareholder approval, size the pool honestly, and issue grant letters that match what was promised. Note that the pool will usually be created pre-money, so the founders bear the dilution.
4. The trademark is real but slowest-burning. File immediately, take legal advice on the Delhi application, and disclose it. A rebrand is survivable. An unowned product is not.
The general lesson: every one of these four was cheap to prevent and expensive to fix. Diligence does not create problems, it discovers them.

body.title: Pre-raise legal readiness
steps: Private limited company incorporated, with a company bank account and an appointed statutory auditor.
Founders' agreement signed, with four-year vesting, a one-year cliff and buyback terms for unvested shares.
IP assignment and confidentiality clauses signed by every founder, employee, intern and contractor.
Trademark applied for, and domains, cloud, code repositories and app store accounts held in the company's name.
Cap table reconciled to share certificates, the register of members and allotment filings with the Registrar.
ESOP scheme approved by the board and shareholders, with grant letters issued, and no informal promises outstanding.
ROC annual filings, GST and TDS returns up to date, with the last two years' accounts audited.
DPIIT recognition obtained, if eligible, and any related-party arrangements disclosed in writing.

body.title: The first year of vesting
body.textWithBlank: Under a standard four-year founder vesting schedule, a founder who leaves before completing the one-year ___ keeps no shares at all.
body.explanation: The cliff protects the company from someone leaving after a few months with a permanent stake. After the cliff, vesting usually continues monthly until the end of year four.

cards.definition: The standard Indian structure for funded startups, and the only common one that can issue equity shares to investors.
Founder shares earned over time, typically four years, with unvested shares bought back at a nominal price if the founder leaves.
The initial period, usually one year, before any shares vest. Leave earlier and nothing is earned.
A written clause transferring ownership of work created by an employee or contractor to the company.
The company's statutory record of who owns its shares, which must reconcile with the cap table and filings.
Free government recognition of an eligible startup, unlocking scheme eligibility, IPR support and self-certification.
Business done with an entity connected to a founder or director, which must be disclosed and priced at arm's length.

points: Equity investors buy shares, so incorporate a private limited company. LLPs and partnerships block institutional rounds.
Sign a founders' agreement with four-year vesting and a one-year cliff before anyone leaves, not after.
Vesting is arithmetic: 30,00,000 shares over four years means 11,25,000 vested at 18 months, and nothing at all before the cliff.
Employment work usually belongs to the company, but freelancer work does not unless a contract assigns it. Check every contractor.
The cap table must reconcile exactly with share certificates, the register of members and Registrar filings.
Never promise equity or ESOPs informally. Grant them only through an approved scheme with signed letters.
DPIIT recognition is free and unlocks scheme eligibility, IPR support and self-certification, but the tax holiday is a separate approval.
Every common diligence problem is cheap to prevent and expensive to fix once a term sheet is on the table.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Company law, DPIIT scheme conditions, dematerialisation requirements and income tax provisions change, and the applicable section references have shifted with the new income tax legislation. Verify current requirements on official sources and take advice from a qualified company secretary, lawyer or tax professional before acting. Zenta Labs and the other examples are illustrative.
